title: Data Engineering, Machine Learning and Model Evaluation · Text documents
summary: How well CEREBRO searches, groups topics and answers questions — tested on public benchmarks on my own GPU. With the models it was designed for, search scores 0.73 (nDCG@10), three times what the live setup scores today.
meta: Python · PyTorch · scikit-learn · Ollama · PostgreSQL · FastAPI
Ubuntu Linux · NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM)

paragraphs: CEREBRO stores your documents, links related topics in a Galaxy, and answers questions with citations — all with models running locally. It doesn't train those models, so the real question is how well it uses them.
I tested three things on public benchmarks: search, topic grouping, and answering. The tests run CEREBRO's own code, not a copy of it.

Each test ran twice — once with the models the live site uses, once with the models it was built for. That's how I found the live site had no embedding model and had quietly fallen back to a basic one.

blocks.label: Why a separate setup.
blocks.text: Adding an embedding model to the live site would make it re-index everything. So the designed models ran next to it, not inside it.

paragraphs: Public data, labelled by other people — so no private documents, and no way to grade my own homework.

blocks.label: Scope.
blocks.text: Covers text documents only: PDF, Word (.docx), PowerPoint (.pptx), plain text and Markdown — the formats CEREBRO accepts. No images, audio, video or spreadsheets.

paragraphs: Email headers, signatures and quoted replies came out first — otherwise a model learns the sender, not the subject. Then I removed empty posts, duplicates, and any test post that copied a training post.

2 · Splitting documents to fit the model

paragraphs: Documents are split into chunks the embedding model can read (502 tokens max). 5,183 abstracts became 12,146 chunks; the largest was 447 tokens, so nothing overflowed.
Forum posts are messier: 18.4% were too long, so CEREBRO split them, embedded each piece and averaged the result — nothing cut off, nothing rejected.

blocks.caption: Characters per chunk. Most fill close to the budget.

paragraphs: 300 scientific claims, each with abstracts that experts marked relevant. Does search put those near the top? CEREBRO combines a keyword search with a meaning-based search.

blocks.caption: Same code — only the embedding model changes.

blocks.title: Each search method on its own
blocks.caption: nDCG@10 — higher is better. Full figures in the table.

blocks.label: Keyword search finds almost nothing.
blocks.text: It requires every word to match, and these queries are full sentences — 286 of 300 got zero results. A search that lets any word match scored 0.64.

paragraphs: Are relevant abstracts simply more similar to the question? With mxbai, yes — they separate almost perfectly (AUC 0.99). The live hashing model manages 0.78.

blocks.title: Similarity: relevant vs not
blocks.caption: mxbai. Each group shown as a share of itself.

blocks.title: How well similarity alone sorts results
blocks.caption: ROC curve — the closer to the top-left corner, the better.

paragraphs: The Galaxy links topics that are more alike than usual. That only works if the model understands subjects. With mxbai, posts on the same topic score 0.55 on average vs 0.42 across topics. The hashing model barely tells them apart (0.23 vs 0.21).

blocks.title: Can similarity tell topics apart?
blocks.caption: ROC curve for 'same topic or not'.

blocks.text: The Galaxy's linking rule, put to the test

blocks.title: How similar each topic is to every other
blocks.caption: Average similarity between topics. The Galaxy links a pair when it scores above 0.85 (the typical pair is 0.76).

paragraphs: Nearly every link makes sense to a person — the religion groups, PC and Mac hardware, cars and motorcycles. The rule never saw the labels, so this is a fair check.

blocks.title: Posts in two dimensions (PCA)
blocks.caption: 1,500 posts. Each family is outlined and named; 'For sale' is grey. Two dimensions keep only 12.9% of the detail, so neighbours overlap.

blocks.title: How much detail a few dimensions keep
blocks.caption: Embeddings pack meaning into few dimensions; word counts (TF-IDF) spread it thin.

paragraphs: Can a model learn the topic from these representations? Every model got the same data: 9,821 posts to learn from, 1,092 to tune on, and 7,159 held back for the final test.

blocks.title: Test results by model
blocks.caption: Macro-F1 (bar) and accuracy. qwen3 had no training — it just picked from the list.

paragraphs: The embedding does the heavy lifting: four different models on mxbai land within 0.03 of each other. Even the Galaxy's simple no-training rule scores 0.70. On the hashing model, nothing beats 0.32.

A small neural network (535,060 parameters) trained in PyTorch on the GPU. Training stopped once it began to overfit and kept the best version (epoch 3). It took 0.46 seconds and 72 MB of GPU memory. It's an experiment — CEREBRO doesn't ship it.

blocks.title: Training and validation loss
blocks.caption: Validation loss is lowest at epoch 3, so that version was kept.

blocks.title: Training and validation accuracy
blocks.caption: Validation accuracy kept inching up (81% → 83%), but the model was getting overconfident. Stopping early traded 1.5 points for more honest confidence.

blocks.title: Confusion matrix
blocks.caption: Rows are the true topic; numbers are the % of that topic. The diagonal is correct.

blocks.title: Most common mix-ups
blocks.caption: The same pairs the Galaxy links — topics that genuinely overlap.

blocks.title: Is its confidence honest?
blocks.caption: When it says 70%, it's right about 70% of the time (calibration error 0.009).

blocks.caption: Its most useful words for telling topics apart.

paragraphs: Ask CEREBRO should answer only from your documents — and say so when they don't have the answer. Each question came with six passages, exactly as Ask CEREBRO would give them.

blocks.title: Questions that have an answer
blocks.caption: Both models find the answer about equally often (79% vs 80%). The difference is citing: qwen3 points to the right source 93% of the time.

blocks.label: The weak spot.
blocks.text: Both models usually answer anyway, often from general knowledge. CEREBRO's own 'no answer' check also misses common phrasings like 'the documents don't specify', so it under-counts.

items: Install the designed embedding model. Search jumps from 0.23 to 0.73. Needs a planned re-index.
Let keyword search match any word. Today 286 of 300 full-sentence searches return nothing.
Teach Ask CEREBRO to say 'I don't know' — and catch it when it does.
Set the model's context size explicitly. Two long prompts were cut off.
Topic suggestions from embeddings look ready: 0.70 with no training, 0.73 with a half-second of training.

paragraphs: One command on my server runs everything and saves an evidence archive. Every number here comes from those archives, checked file by file against their fingerprints (SHA-256). Running the live setup twice gave identical results.
